title: Texas Votes November 3. The Deadlines Start Before Election Day.
thumbnailMessage: Texas Votes November 3. Registration Ends October 5.
summary: Texas voter registration closes October 5 for the November 3 election. Here are the official dates, where to check your registration, and the records to watch before voting begins.
content:
Texas residents have a concrete date to put on the calendar: October 5, 2026. The Texas secretary of state lists that as the registration deadline for the November 3 general election. Election Day is the finish line for a process that starts much earlier.

This is a public-information guide, checked against the state’s published calendar on September 7. The linked state and county resources remain the place to confirm your individual registration and voting arrangements.

## The dates that matter

According to the secretary of state’s 2026 election dates, in-person early voting runs October 19 through October 30. The early voting clerk must receive an application for a ballot by mail by October 23. That is an application-receipt deadline, not the deadline to return a voted ballot. Election Day is Tuesday, November 3.

Mail voting has separate eligibility and return rules. Check the official instructions and your county election office before relying on that option. A social-media graphic is not a substitute for the current election notice.

## Check your registration at the source

VoteTexas.gov links directly to the state’s registration lookup and county voter registrars. Use those tools to check your own record. The page also links to registration applications and the state’s update process for people who have moved or changed their name. Follow the instructions for the specific transaction; opening a form does not mean a registration application has been completed.

The state cautions that postal collection and postmark dates can differ. Its registration page recommends submitting early and explains how to request a manual postmark at a postal retail counter. If a deadline or registration status is unclear, contact the county registrar now.

## A public record to watch in September

The November election-law calendar identifies September 16 as the date for public logic-and-accuracy and tabulation testing, with website notice at least 48 hours beforehand. The calendar also describes separate testing requirements for electronic pollbooks before early voting. These are different checks; do not collapse them into one event.

Look for your election office’s actual notice, location, and instructions. A scheduled test is not proof that it occurred. A test record is not a claim that a system can never fail. If you want to understand what was checked, start with the notice and resulting records.

## RepWatchr commentary: ask for something you can check

Public confidence deserves more than a slogan from either party. Give people the dates, the notices, and a clear explanation of the process. When something is missing, ask for it. When something is wrong, preserve the source and request a correction.

That same standard belongs on the candidate side. Ask what an official actually voted on, what a proposal costs, and where the supporting document can be read. A campaign answer becomes useful when an ordinary person can check it.

RepWatchr’s community feedback is separate from an official election. A response on this website does not register a voter, cast a government ballot, or establish what an entire district believes. Keeping those distinctions clear makes the information more useful.

Your next three moves are straightforward: check your registration through the official state resources, save your county’s current election page, and start a short list of the local decisions and candidate questions you want answered before November.
